summary: Describes what mailing list software should do once email addresses can contain non-ASCII characters (internationalized addresses). It gives specific recommendations for how lists should behave in various situations, such as when members or the list itself use such addresses. It is an experimental specification. It was replaced by RFC 6783.

plainLanguage.summary: A mailing list is like a club that copies every letter to all members. This explains how the club should cope when some members' addresses are written with letters from other alphabets.

questions: how do mailing lists handle internationalized email addresses
how should lists handle mixed ascii and non-ascii members
subtitle: Handling international addresses in mailing list operations

tldr.problem: Email can now use addresses with non-ASCII characters, but mailing list software needs guidance on how to handle these addresses safely when copying messages to multiple subscribers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies requirements for how lists should accept, deliver, and downgrade messages with internationalized addresses, including when and how to request alternative ASCII versions of addresses.
tldr.outcome: Lists can properly support non-ASCII addresses for subscribers and senders without breaking delivery to members who use ASCII-only systems. This RFC was replaced by RFC 6783.

today: RFC 5983 is an Experimental specification and has been replaced by RFC 6783. It addressed the design challenge of how mailing lists should handle internationalized email addresses when delivering to subscribers with varying levels of support for non-ASCII characters.

sections.title: The Challenge of Internationalized Addresses
sections.content:
Internationalized email addresses let users write email addresses in their own language or script, like cyrillic or Arabic letters. When mailing lists distribute messages, they face a new problem: some subscribers use modern systems that understand these non-ASCII addresses, while others use older systems that only understand traditional ASCII addresses (a-z, 0-9, @).

A mailing list must decide how to handle messages from non-ASCII addresses and forward them to a mix of modern and legacy subscribers. The list also needs to pick what address it uses as the return path for error messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a club that sends copies of letters to all members, but some members have names written in different alphabets. The club needs rules for handling these different names without confusing any member.

sections.title: Handling Messages and Addresses
sections.content:
When a mailing list receives a message from someone with an internationalized address and needs to send it to subscribers who may not support non-ASCII characters, the message must be downgraded—converted to a form that uses only ASCII. But downgrading only works if the sender or list has an ASCII alternative address available.

The RFC recommends that if a list has an internationalized submission or return-path address, it SHOULD register an ASCII alternative for that address. If a list accepts subscribers with internationalized addresses, it MAY require them to provide an ASCII alternative. If a list accepts UTF8SMTP messages (the modern email protocol that supports non-ASCII characters), its incoming mail servers must be prepared for them.
sections.plainLanguage: If you need to send a letter to old mailboxes that can't read fancy letters, you need a regular version of that address to send it to instead. The list should ask members for a backup ASCII address just in case.

sections.title: List-Specific Header Fields
sections.content:
Mailing lists add special header fields to outgoing messages, such as List-Id, List-Help, List-Unsubscribe, and List-Post. These fields contain URLs and mailto addresses that email clients use to help subscribers manage their membership.

When a list uses internationalized addresses in these fields, it should also provide ASCII-encoded equivalents. The RFC notes that the List-ID field is special: email clients use it to filter and organize messages, so non-ASCII values that are percent-encoded might not be recognizable to users or easy for them to type. The List-ID should remain stable even if the list moves to a new server.
sections.plainLanguage: The list adds buttons and labels to messages so members can reply or unsubscribe easily. When using fancy letters, the list should provide regular versions too, so all email readers understand them.

sections.title: Security and Best Practices
sections.content:
Using both an internationalized address and an ASCII alternative for the same entity creates a potential security risk. An attacker could bind a non-ASCII address and an ASCII address together and use the alias to deny someone else admission to the mailing list, or to frame the wrong person for sending a message. List administrators must be careful when implementing authorization features like subscription approval, sender filtering, and other list controls.

A list operator might choose to reject messages from internationalized addresses that lack an ASCII alternative, to avoid delivery failures when the message must be downgraded. This trade-off improves reliability but restricts who can send to the list.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone has two versions of their address (fancy and regular), someone bad could try to trick the list by pretending both addresses belong to different people. List managers need to be careful about who they allow to send.

sections.title: Where This Stands Now
sections.content: RFC 5983 is an Experimental specification and was replaced by RFC 6783, which updated the recommendations. The core challenge—balancing support for internationalized addresses with backward compatibility for ASCII-only systems—remains important for mailing list operators deploying modern email infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: This document was a first attempt to solve the problem and has been superseded by a newer version, but the issues it raises are still relevant.
